title: Why Doesn't a Steel Ship Sink?
description:
Steel sinks. So why does a 200,000-ton steel ship float without even trying? The answer has nothing to do with the metal itself — it's about a hollow shape, displaced water, and a rule that quietly works against you the moment you load on too much weight.

scenes.narration: Here's a question that doesn't seem to add up.

visual.text: A question that doesn't add up.

scenes.narration: A solid block of steel sinks instantly.
But a steel ship floats perfectly.
The answer has nothing to do with the steel itself.
It's about how much space that steel takes up.
A ship's hull is mostly hollow — air, cargo space, empty rooms.
That hollow space lets the ship displace a huge amount of water.

visual.text: It displaces a huge amount of water.

scenes.narration: Water pushes back exactly as hard as the weight it displaced.
If that push-back can support the ship's full weight, it floats.
Not the density of the steel — the average density of the whole ship.
Load too much cargo, and that balance shifts — cross the line, and it sinks.

visual.text: Cross the line, and it sinks.
